FOUND: At closing, young men in their twenties shout at the takeaway's window on the Parade. No words carry, only the noise and Lily's face. Peter says it is nothing. Lily, handing Tom his change: "Come at closing, if you're passing. The window by the Tivoli's side door." [invented: the Tivoli as landmark]

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Lily has served Tom twice. Waits three closing times, then it goes on without him.

STEPS:
1. First closing, the pavement opposite the window: Tom sees the men and Lily's face. He can cross or walk on.
2. The next closing, inside at the counter: Tom stands there and orders slowly. He can also bring Ron to stand by the door.
3. The corner by the Tivoli's side door: Tom can speak quietly to the men, or shame their leader before the Parade crowd.

ENDINGS:
- Presence: Tom or Ron at the counter, and the men drift off. Lily remembers who stood there and says so to the regulars.
- Humiliation: the leader is shamed in front of the Parade. It ends, and Danny's crew notices.
- Nothing: it goes on, and the regulars see him not see it.

The town keeps who stood at the counter.

IF IT GOES WRONG: If Tom misses all three closings or does nothing, the shouting continues. Lily serves him politely but coolly, and Peter still says it is nothing. [invented] The regulars remember that he was there and did not act. The men are never heard voicing anything and are never rewarded.

LEDGER LINES:
- Lily Tang wants someone at the takeaway counter at closing, on the Parade by the Tivoli's side door. Men keep shouting at the window.
- Closing at the Tangs' is quiet tonight. Lily knows who stood at the counter, and the Parade will hear about it by morning.

INVENTIONS

Sheila Dunn was born in 1937 in a terraced street in a mill town inland, a day's bus ride from Meridian [invented]. At eighteen, in 1955, she was a ledger clerk at a coal merchant's there [invented]. At twenty she came to Meridian for a clerk's place at a shipping agent's office in the Exchange [invented]. She took a room in the Hook because it was cheap, and she has not lived anywhere else since. The agent's office hired cars with drivers for its visitors, and that is how she first heard the name Mickey Suddaby [invented].

In 1959, aged twenty-two, she answered a card in the window on Quay Street. In 1959 Mickey's was a car-hire firm with a yard, a few saloons and a handful of drivers, never a pub [invented]. It became a minicab office when that trade came in, around 1961 [invented]. His clerk had left and the figures were a mess. She sorted them in a week and never left. That is the thirty-one years.

She married a docker, and he died in 1982 [invented]. She lives on in a council flat on the edge of Copper Row [invented]. She smokes, wears dentures, and has her hair set every Saturday afternoon [invented]. She does not discuss any of it.

Mickey, to her, was a careless man with paper and a careful man with people. He did things quietly and expected them to stay quiet. She marks in the book any money the office pays out, and she kept his books accordingly: the day book, the fare book, and the other one. She knows which were real. She says so to no one. The key to Mickey's own room, the locked door at the back, is on her ring, and she has not turned it since he died. She found out the way the street did, when Ron came in from the rank white-faced. The doctor said his heart. She has no reason to say otherwise and says nothing.

Ron Kirby is the person she is closest to in the office, because Ron is the only other one who was there for all of it. He worked the docks until 1989 and Mickey kept him on for the door and the rank. She has watched him since the funeral. Two nights before Mickey died she saw Ron arguing with a stranger in the yard behind the office. She knows what she saw and no more, and she has not asked Ron about it. She has not decided whether that is loyalty or cowardice.

Ada keeps a window across the street, and Sheila has tea there in the afternoons. Sheila knows things Mickey did for people without their knowing, and she keeps them unless asked straight. She nods to Rita on the pawn step, to Hal in the coin shop that sells no coins, and to Father Walsh, whose chapel buried Mickey. She puts up with Darren Milner, who walks the street selling nothing anyone can name, and who owes the office money she has written down. She knows Alison Sedman and June Suddaby only a little. June came for the funeral and wants nothing, which Sheila respects. On Thursdays she stops at the newsagent's pension counter, where Edith Stockill trusts her judgement of people more than her own [invented that Sheila's errand there is a regular call on Edith].

July 1989 touched her through the book. The dock labour scheme ended, and more than half the registered dockers' jobs went. The office had run on dockers' fares and dockers' tabs, and the tabs stopped being paid. The phone rings more than it used to and it is rarely good news. The book of debts is in her hand, and she knows which will never be collected. Last November the importer's warehouse burned on a Saturday night. She keeps what she knows of it behind her face.

Her day is plain. She is in at nine and does the figures. At noon she walks to the fish front for her dinner, is back at one, and sits on Rita's step at five with a cigarette before going home at six. On Thursdays she is at the pension counter first and in the office at ten. On Saturdays she finishes at one, and Sundays she does not work, though the office opens. The office opens at seven and runs until the night driver goes home at three. She has never kept those hours and has never needed to.

She wants three things. She wants the office to go on. She wants to keep her place in it, which she says is the same thing. And she wants to know what kind of man Mickey's nephew is before the office is his in more than law. She promised Mickey she would size up whoever inherited, and she means to do it properly. He arrived with one suitcase and a let

FOUND: Karen Grummitt, at the ferry's ticket window, once she has sold Tom a ticket or seen him at the landing twice, says quietly: "I need a car at five on Thursday, with my case, and not a word to Mrs Rennison. I owe her a fortnight."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Karen has sold Tom a ticket or seen him at the landing twice. She waits until Thursday, 5:00.

STEPS:
1. Ticket window, ferry landing. Karen names the time and the secret. Tom can agree, refuse, or ask why.
2. Mickey's office, Quay Street. Pauline Kitching, on the radio, can book the car. A driver from the rank can be sent [invented]. Tom never drives.
3. Sylvia Rennison

Ron Kirby was born in 1932 and turned eighteen in 1950, in a terraced street in a dock town up the coast from Meridian [invented]. That year he went to work in a coal yard, humping sacks, until his call-up came [invented]. He did his two years of national service in a ship's stores party, which is where the blue tattoos on his hands and forearms come from [invented]. He came back to a job he did not want, labouring for a builder's firm in Meridian [invented]. In 1959 a man he had met on a site got him a registered card on the Meridian quay [invented]. He worked there for thirty years, on the quayside and in the sheds, a big, slow, patient man the gangs were glad to have behind them. He rolled his own cigarettes through all of it and still does [invented]. He never married and has lived alone for most of his adult life, in two rented rooms in a terrace off Tannery Row in Ironside [invented]. He has no phone there and uses the box on the corner of Quay Street.

He knew Mickey Suddaby the way the quay knew him: as the man whose cabs ran the shifts to the dock gates when the buses didn't [invented]. The two were never friends in those years. Ron respected Mickey because Mickey paid on the day he said he would. In July 1989 the dock labour scheme ended, and more than half the registered men lost their work. Ron was one of them. He says it ended "with a letter" and does not say much more. Within the week Mickey had put him on the door and the rank of the minicab office on Quay Street, at a wage that was less than a docker's and paid in cash. Ron has not forgotten it. His loyalty is real, but he would tell you himself that it is also a wage.

Mickey, as Ron knew him, was a tidy, close-mouthed man who liked things in their places, with a book for every fare and a radio always on. They shared a Friday order at the Tangs' takeaway, two of number nine, every Friday. Ask Ron about it and he goes quiet, then says "Fridays, aye." He found Mickey dead at the office early one morning, when he came on at the rank, and the doctor said it was his heart. Nobody has suggested otherwise. In the week Mickey died, Ron took Mickey's watch to Rita's pawn shop and pawned it to pay for the funeral flowers [invented]. He means to get it back when he can [invented]. He has told no one, including Sheila. Rita keeps tickets and her own counsel. He stood at the back of Father Walsh's chapel for the funeral.

On Quay Street he is close to Sheila Dunn, who has been at Mickey's since she was twenty-two and is usually in the office in the afternoons. They have an easy, grumbling understanding [invented]. He knows Darren Milner well, as everyone does, and Ada in her window, who has never needed to be told who goes by. He nods to Rita and Hal and Father Walsh. On the quay he still has a dock hand, a crane driver and a net mender he talks to, a little, about nothing. The boarding house knows him as the man to send for a word with a lodger behind on his rent. He has done it, quietly and without a hand raised, and he is paid in goodwill and an occasional meal [invented]. Shopkeepers on the street feel easier with him standing near a door.

His day runs to a pattern. At seven he is in the cafe across the street, with the evening paper from the night before folded in his coat pocket and a tea in front of him. At eight he is on the rank, watching the pavement and the yard gate. At noon he walks to the fish front for his dinner, and he is back on the rank at one. At five he goes down to the quay and stands there as long as the weather lets him, which is a habit more than an errand. From seven he is in the office, in earshot of the radio, until he goes home at eleven. On Sundays he works an allotment from ten till one and grows leeks and potatoes on it [invented]. He is back at the office at seven in the evening as on any other night. A tenner is folded in his top pocket and he is always a little short of the next one.

What he wants is to be kept on, at any money, and to go on being the man at the door. He is not sentimental about that. He fears being let go a second time by a stranger who owns the place and does not know him. He had never met Mickey's nephew before he came, and Mickey spoke of him only now and then. So Ron watches him the way he watches the street, and he will tell the new owner what he has seen. He has no appetite for trouble that nobody is paying for. He respects strength first and cash after it, and he has not yet decided which this man has.

INVENTIONS:
- Born in a dock town up the coast
- Coal yard job at eighteen
- National service in a ship's stores party, source of the tattoos
- Builder's labouring after service
- Registered on the quay in 1959 through a man from the site
- Rolls his own cigarettes
- Never married, lives alone
- Two rented rooms in a terrace off Tannery Row, Ironside
- Mickey's cabs ran dock shift runs
- Mickey as tidy, close-mouthed
- Ron pawned the watch intending to redeem it
- Told no one, Sheila included, about the pawn
- Rita keeps her own counsel
- Stood at the back of the chapel for the funeral
- Easy, grumbling understanding with Sheila
- Talks with the dock hand, crane driver and net mender about nothing
- Has done the boarding-house "word" quietly, paid in goodwill and meals
- Walks to the fish front for his dinner
- Goes to the quay at five out of habit
- Sunday allotment grows leeks and potatoes
- Wage under a docker's, in cash

FOUND: Brenda Laverack, loud at her fish-shop counter: "My dawn order on the fish dock's coming up short, and somebody's collecting it under my name. Look at the railing by the weigh-in, if you've got the stomach for it."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Tom has spoken to Brenda once. She waits 3 dawns, then stops waiting.

STEPS:
1. The fish market railing at dawn: Brenda is buying, and the chalked box count is a few short. Tom can watch, count for himself, or ask her.
2. The weigh-in by the railing: the porter who signs for her boxes. Tom can ask him, watch where the missing boxes go, or let him see he is watched.
3. The back of the fish dock: the syndicate's man who takes the porters' cut. Tom can lean on him, bargain with him, or send word to the Widow's people.

ENDINGS:
- Catch the porter: Tom deals with him himself, by a word or by fists. The dock sees it, and Brenda hears how it was done.
- Pay quietly: Tom covers Brenda's loss and says nothing. Brenda knows it was him, and the porter carries on.
- Ask the Widow's people: it is sorted at once. The dock now knows whose favour Tom asked.

IF IT GOES WRONG: The porter sees Tom coming and the dock closes ranks. Nobody will count a box in front of him, and Brenda tells everyone he tried.

THE TOWN KEEPS: Brenda's version, which the whole parade hears by noon.

LEDGER LINES:
- Brenda Laverack's fish order is coming up short at the market railing on the fish dock, and someone signs for it in her name.
- The porter who signs Brenda's boxes works the weigh-in by the railing. The syndicate's man takes the porters' cut behind the dock.

INVENTIONS:
- The count is chalked up at the railing, so a shortfall can be seen [invented].
- The porter and the syndicate's man are left unnamed, to be cast when built [invented].

FOUND: Dawn Pybus, clipboard in hand, on Ada's step across from the cab office [invented]. She says, "It's gone up, love. Ada's not said a word, and I'd sooner you heard it from me." Offered only once Ada's tea is past.

OFFERED / WAITS: offered when Ada's tea is past (the outline's first test). Waits until the next rent day.

STEPS:
1. Ada's step, Quay Street: Dawn explains the rise. Tom can press her for the figure or leave it.
2. The cab office: Tom asks Sheila, who admits Mickey paid the difference without Ada knowing.
3. The agent's counter, a firm in the Exchange: Tom can ask what is owed, or pay the difference in cash [invented].
4. Rent day, Ada's step: Dawn comes round again. Tom decides what Ada is told.

ENDINGS:
- Pay in secret: Ada never knows. Sheila does, and it counts. The street sees her still at her window.
- Tell Ada: she refuses his money and her tea goes cold, or she takes it and is ashamed. Which she does follows how she rated him after the tea [invented]. Either way she knows, and Dawn and Sheila know she knows.
- Let it stop: Ada moves her chair from the window to the back room. The street notices its watcher gone.

The town keeps who keeps Ada at her window.

IF IT GOES WRONG: if rent day passes with nothing done, the story ends as "let it stop". The empty window is the world state, and

FOUND
Outside Mickey's on Quay Street, by the rank, Darren has a crate at his feet and a grin: "Ten each to you. I owe you anyway." Ada watches from her window.

OFFERED / WAITS
Offered when Darren owes the office and Tom has money on him. Darren waits 2 town hours, then "stops waiting" and takes the crate elsewhere.

STEPS
1. Pavement outside Mickey's, by the rank. Darren, the crate, Ron at the door. Tom can look the radios over, ask where they came from (Darren says "a lorry, doesn't matter which"), or tune one.
2. Same spot. Darren haggles. Tom can pay ten pounds [invented] for one, walk away, or say the debt comes off first.
3. If he presses the debt: Darren hands over radios against it and Sheila marks the book down. [invented]
4. Later, in the office. The radio sits on a shelf where Pauline and the drivers can see it.

ENDINGS
- Buy one: it works for a week, then dies. Ron, Ada and Darren know Tom bought from Darren.
- Refuse: Darren shrugs and goes.

FOUND: Tom comes by the caff for tea and finds Grace Rinaldi's front window boarded. She will not say who. "Round the corner from the boarded pub on Quay Street, that's where he'll be hanging about [invented]. No police, and no fists either."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Grace knows Tom by name. She waits until the glazier comes (2 days).

STEPS:
1. The caff counter: Grace, and whoever is eating. Tom can ask who did it, or offer to see to it. She answers only with the rule.
2. Tracey Scarth's market stall in Copper Row [invented]: she sews as she talks. She saw a young man running, only a shape and a pace. Tom can press her or take what she gives.
3. The corner by the boarded pub: the newest of Danny Cammack's crew, about twenty. Tom can talk, threaten, bring him, hand him over or hit him.

ENDINGS:
- Grace's way: Tom brings him to wash her pots for a week. The street knows Tom did it Grace's way, and Grace forgets nobody.
- Ellis: Tom hands him to DS Ellis. Grace calls it police, which she said not to, and says so at the counter.
- Fists: Tom hurts him. Grace bars Tom from the caff and says why.

FOUND: Sylvia Rennison, in her slippers on the boarding house step by the ferry landing [invented]: "Three weeks behind, he is, and one of Danny Cammack's. Mickey would have had a word."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Tom has stopped by the boarding house's step. She waits until Friday.

STEPS:
1. Boarding house step: Sylvia gives the sum, three weeks, £54 [invented]. Tom can ask questions, promise nothing, or walk on.
2. Mickey's, on Quay Street: Ron Kirby and Sheila Dunn are there. Ron says Mickey "had a word" and offers to go. Sheila says what the till can spare. Tom can ask either.
3. Quay Street, any time before Friday: Tom may see the lodger leave the boarding house. He can speak to him or let him pass.
4. Boarding house step, Friday: Sylvia asks for his answer. Tom sends Ron, pays her himself, or refuses.

ENDINGS:
- Send Ron: the rent is paid. Danny's crew hears that Mickey's is still Mickey's.
- Pay it yourself: Sylvia is grateful and tells nobody, then tells everybody. The street knows Tom settles other people's bills.
- Refuse, "I'm not Mickey": Sylvia repeats it word for word. The town keeps the phrase Tom used.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Friday passes with no answer and Sylvia "stopped waiting". She puts the lodger's case on the step, and the street says Mickey's let it lie. Danny's crew h

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered the Saturday

FOUND: Mid-call at the radio desk in Mickey's on Quay Street, Pauline Kitching calls to whoever is at the counter: "Take that phone a minute. She wants a car for the doctor's at ten and she'll only give her name to me."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Tom is behind the counter while Pauline is on another call. The call wa

FOUND: Pauline takes a call on the office phone and passes it to Tom. Susan Coverdale says: "I come off at the Harbour Board gate, by the ferry landing, gone eleven. Could a car wait for me there?" She has seen him on the quay at night and says nothing more. [invented: the gate as her finishing point, and the call coming to the office]

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Susan has seen Tom at the landing at night. She waits three late turns.

STEPS:
1. Harbour Board gate, ferry landing: Terry Hodgson drives, with Susan in the back. Tom may ride in front or leave it to Terry. She talks about the quay, and he can answer plainly or say little.
2. Same gate, a second night: she asks about the cars and the radio. Tom may be along or not.
3. Her door, past Rita's: she mentions something she noticed on the quay. Tom can keep it, use it, or end the fares.

ENDINGS:
- Straight rides, straight talk: Tom answers honestly. Susan tells colleagues and people she trusts that he is honest. The town keeps her word as a customs officer's opinion.
- Use her talk for the night business: she notices that too. Colleagues hear he asks questions of a careful woman, and the town keeps that.
- Refuse her fares: she walks home, and the street keeps that she was left at the gate.

IF IT GOES WRONG: If Tom misses three late turns, she stops waiting and walks the quay home. Pauline hears of the car that never came, and the street says the office keeps its customs officer standing.

- Susan Coverdale, the customs officer past Rita's, w

FOUND: Rain after dark, Tom in the office. The phone rings and Pauline says, dry: "It's the police. She wants a car. Her own's packed up by the fish market, and she's not happy about it."

OFFERED / WAITS: Raining, after dark, and Ellis has met Tom once. She waits 30 town minutes, then she walks.

STEPS:
1. The radio room, Quay Street. Pauline holds the call and Terry is by the door with his keys. Tom can send Terry, say he'll go too, or tell Pauline to refuse the fare.
2. The cab on Quay Street. If Tom goes, he sits in the back for Ellis's sake, and Terry drives, since Tom never does.
3. By the fish market. Ellis stands beside her dead car in the rain. She gets in, or, if Tom stayed behind, speaks only to Terry.
4. The ride. She names the stop, and Tom can answer, deflect or say little. [invented]

ENDINGS:
- Ride with her: she learns what Tom says and how he says it. Terry, who drove, remembers that she asked and that he answered.
- Terry alone: Terry tells Tom what she asked, or says "nothing" and means it.
- Refused: Ellis walks home in the rain and remembers it.

The town keeps Terry's version, told to Kevin on the rank next morning. [invented]

IF IT GOES WRONG: If the 30 minutes pass or Tom refuses, Ellis walks. She is soaked and cold with Tom, and the rank hears from Terry that the office left a sergeant in the rain. The story continues from there.

LEDGER LINES:
- "Ellis's car has died by the fish market. Pauline says she wants a cab. Terry's keys are in his hand. Decide."
- "Ellis got home by the fish market in the rain, on foot. Terry's already told Kevin

FOUND: Tom passes the newsagent's on Quay Street, a few doors from Mickey's [invented], and Edith Stockill calls him to the pension counter. "You're not from round here, dear, and you've kept your mouth shut. Everybody else round here talks. Sign there for me."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Edith has seen Tom keep something to himself (a deed nobody heard of from him

FOUND: Over a bacon sandwich at Grace Rinaldi's caff, Gary Mawer says: "Your uncle rented a berth at the yard, the one by the slipway. Three months unpaid, and nobody's boat on it." [invented: slipway as landmark]

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once the Widow's people have noticed Tom. Gary waits until the yard's month end.

STEPS:
1. The caff: Tom can press Gary for what he knows, or say nothing and go.
2. The yard, by the slipway: the berth is empty. Gary and Ian Megginson are about, and Tom can ask either of them.
3. The yard office: Tom is shown the bill. He can pay, stall, or ask for it in writing.
4. The same week, at the yard gate: the Widow's man asks

FOUND: Doreen Harland stands at the steam laundry's side door, under its tall chimney [invented], with a stack of hampers and no van: "Your lot could carry these for us. Mickey would have."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Mickey's has a spare car on the rank in daytime. She waits until the laundry's van is mended, 2 days.

STEPS:
1. Laundry side door. Doreen and the hampers. Tom can ask how many a day, where they go [invented], and what she'd pay.
2. Mickey's, Quay Street. Pauline on the radio, Kevin Needham beside the rank. Tom can ask Kevin to take a run, hear him moan, or ask Sheila what it would look like in the book.
3. Back at the side door. Tom gives Doreen his answer: the fare rate, no, or a figure well under it.
4. Next morning, the first run. Kevin drives the hampers out with the office's name on the car. If the price was low, Sheila asks Tom about it.

ENDINGS:
- Take it at the fare rate: clean money goes into the fare book, Kevin and

FOUND: Hal Metcalfe, retired fish-merchant's clerk, has seen Tom on the parade on a Monday and says through the shop door of the coin shop that sells no coins: "It's the company I keep the shop for. Bring the paper on a Monday and I'll talk." The shop stands a few doors from Rita's pawn. [invented]

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered once Hal has seen Tom on the parade on a Monday. He waits every Monday from 10 to 4.

STEPS:
1. The parade, Monday: Hal nods to Tom from the pavement and says his piece. Tom can answer or walk on.
2. Outside the coin shop, Monday between 10 and 4: Tom buys a paper at the newsagent's first. [invented] Without one, Hal is courteous and evasive.
3. Inside the shop, with Hal alone: Tom sits and listens. Hal gives what the street is saying about him, a day before it reaches him, drawn from the simulation's gossip.
4. Tom leaves, and can act on it or ignore it. Hal says "Next Monday, then."

ENDINGS:
- Monday visits: Tom comes each week, sits and hears the talk early. The street sees him go in; Hal remembers everyone's business, Tom's included.
- None: there is no other ending. The story simply repeats.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Tom misses a Monday, or comes without the paper

FOUND: Tom passes the kiosk by the ferry landing [invented] and hears Julie Kettlewell telling anyone near: "Twelve weeks I gave that steam laundry, the one with the tall chimney by the tannery wall [invented], and they've kept my last weeks' money."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when Tom passes the kiosk while Julie is there. She waits 6 town hours, then takes a job across town.

STEPS:
1. The laundry's front office, under the chimney. Nobody will say anything about her pay. Tom can ask, wait, or leave. The owner is out the back.
2. The owner, in his office behind the presses. Tom can ask politely, lean on him, or go away and come back.
3. Doreen Harland, on the early shift at the washing floor, who saw the packets made up in full and says so bluntly. Tom can ask what she saw, and decide whether to use it.
4. Back to Julie, or to Sheila Dunn at the office, to settle it.

ENDINGS:
- Lean on the owner: he pays Julie, then tells Christine Pickering at the harbour office he was threatened. The harbour office knows Mickey's still frightens people.
- Pay Julie from the office: Sheila marks it in the book. Sheila knows, and Julie tells the street Mickey's still looks after its own.
- Give her the office phone beside Pauline Kitching: Pauline, Ron and the rank see who counts as Mickey's own now.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Tom is too slow, or walks away. Julie starts across town, the owner keeps the money, and Doreen tells the washing floor the new owner did n

FOUND: Winifred Duggleby, talking to her ruined flowers, tells Tom: "Rain's coming through over the altar, love, and Dennis Iveson's got the roof's lead in a stack on the warehouse row. Fair's fair, he says."

OFFERED / WAITS: Offered when it has rained two days running and Danny Cammack's crew is on the street (Act II). Waits until Dennis sells the lead on (2 days).

STEPS:
1. The wet altar in the chapel: Winifred and Nora Cronin. Tom can look up at the leak and ask who sold the lead.
2. Dennis Iveson's scales on the old warehouse row: Dennis, jovial, with the stack. Tom can buy it back, ask who sold it, or walk away.
3. The corner by the warehouse row: two of Danny's men. Tom can lean on them, watch them, or take their names to Ellis.

ENDINGS:
- Buy back: Tom pays Dennis, who profits twice and knows it. Dennis tells the row. The parish says from the pulpit that the roof was mended, with no name or a name.
- Lean on the two: they return the money. Danny hears Tom touched his crew. The roof is mended, and the pulpit thanks with no name or a name.
- Give Ellis their names: whoever saw Tom at her car says so. The parish does not thank a grass, and Danny's crew asks who it was.

IF IT GOES WRONG: Dennis sells the lead on and stops waiting. The roof stays open, buckets stand under the altar, and Winifred's flowers rot. Nora and Father Walsh say nothing, and the street says Tom let it drip.

Darren Milner was eighteen in the autumn of 1983, living in a mill town in the north, a coach ride inland from any sea, and he has never said much about it [invented]. That autumn his mother took a job at the steam laundry in Meridian, and he came down with her because a year's training scheme had a place going [invented]. He was placed with a ship chandler's stores on the edge of the Hook, where he learned where things are kept and who comes to collect them [invented]. The year ended and the chandler kept nobody on. Darren has not been on a payroll since. He is twenty-five now. What he did instead he calls "getting about": errands, carrying, finding things, introducing one person to another for a tenner.

The Hook taught him that the docks ran on favours as much as wages. Through the middle of the decade he was useful to men who had money and no time: dockers, a crane driver, a customs assistant who liked to be told things as well as tell them [invented]. He fetched, he passed on messages, and he learned that a rumour carried to the right person was worth more than most things he could carry in his hands. He started leaving messages with the dispatcher at Mickey's because nobody could ever reach him directly, and the dispatcher let him. That was how he came to Mickey.

Mickey Suddaby was not kind to him, exactly. He was consistent. He let Darren stand under the rank's cover when it rained, lent him a tenner when the pager was about to be cut off, and wrote the loan down in the office book every time, in front of him, so that Darren could never say it had been forgotten. Darren owed Mickey's money when Mickey died, and still does; the sum is small and he is not saying how small [invented]. He took it as respect that he was written down. Mickey also let him sleep across the back seat of the spare car in the yard on nights when going home was worse than staying out. Ron Kirby knew and said nothing [invented]. Mickey spoke of his sister's son now and then, as a man who existed, and Darren never learned more than that.

Darren is close to the people who see him most. He knows Ron well, from the door and the rank, and the night driver. Sheila Dunn he knows well too, from the afternoons at Mickey's, and she tolerates him as she tolerates damp. Alison Sedman, out on her rounds, treats him as a source and says so. Ada, at her window, knows him a little. Further out are the ferryman, the scrap dealer and the night watchman on the warehouse row, the pawn shop's staff, the locksmith, the seamstress at the laundry, Hal, and a long tail of cousins. He knows everyone, and none of them would swear to him.

July 1989 hit him sideways. He was never a registered docker, but the men who were had been his customers and his news. When more than half the registered jobs went, the tenners stopped, the talk went quiet, and the crowd at the quay thinned to the few who could not leave. Ron Kirby was let go. Mickey's trade fell off. Darren found that gossip is worth less when nobody has money to act on it, and he has been working the night crowd harder ever since.

His mother's house is a bus ride from the Hook, in Ironside, and he is registered there, eats there, and is lectured there [invented]. On the nights he sleeps in the yard he has either missed the last bus or has decided that the front door will go badly. The street can believe both. His mother does not ask.
